text.p: Base metal prices continued to trend lower during Friday afternoon LME trading, as confirmation of bearish chart signals prompted general liquidation, traders said. All the markets finished in the minus column, and further losses will likely be sustained next week as investment funds are sucked in to add to existing short positions.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index fell 0.43 points to finish at 242.71.

LME copper was unable to hold on to $2,300, and after some desultory business in the official rings, a lower New York trend sent prices under important chart support at $2,280. The backwardation also narrowed from above $40 to around $38, basis cash/threes. Last business was at $2,269 a tonne, down $33 from Thursday's kerb close.
Aluminium similarly fell away, underlining persistent failures at or near $1,600 recently, and by the close of the kerb prices were $22 easier at $1,564 and seen heading for $1,550.
Nickel prices remained above their lows during the afternoon, although bearish charts continued to weigh on the market. The market closed at $7,250, down $25.

Lead continued to trade near early 18-month lows of $625, concluding $12 easier at $627, with fundamentals giving scant support. Physicals are slow at present, and the unseasonably mild weather in Northern Europe does not bode well for battery manufacturer offtake, they said.
Zinc drifted lower with the main trend, ending at $1,232, a loss of $12. However, the fundamental picture is fairly constructive, which should restrict further declines.
Tin eased to $5,630, down $60, while alloy was marked down to $1,455/60 a tonne, a loss of $15.

New York precious metals futures ended lower Friday, as funds sold and recent support levels broke, following worse-than-expected U.S. March PPI and retail sales data which drove U.S. bill and bond yields sharply higher. "With the market and the Fed driving real interest rates higher, precious metals look less attractive, while the weakness in the stock market is not yet pronounced enough to encourage a move into gold," Chase

Manhattan New York managing director Dinsa Mehta said. COMEX June gold ended down $1.60 at $349.30, after seeing an intraday low at $348.00, as the contract tested the bottom of the $348.30-358.00 range of the past month. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $346.60/10, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $347.95 and the New York close Thursday around $348.40/90.

Harsh winter-like weather during springtime in the U.S. plus dry weather in Europe boosted CBOT wheat futures to a strongly higher close, traders said. "We do have dynamics changing quite a bit for wheat," said Bob Lekberg, grains and oilseed analyst for Chicago-based trade house Goldenberg Hehmeyer. "There's a potential disruption in plantings in the northern U.S. spring wheat area and cold weather is coming into the (hard red) winter area." Portions of the HRW crop is vulnerable to winterkill. Wheat closed one to 10-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with May up 10 at $4.03 and July up 10-1/4 at $4.08-1/4.

NYMEX crude ended slightly lower Friday as an early boost from diplomatic tensions between European Union (EU) countries and Iran faded late session since the row had no immediate impact on supply, traders said. "I think the feeling is that if it were that serious, the EU would impose sanctions, but they haven't. In any case, a situation like that would affect Brent more, and Brent failed to hold gains too," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York. May crude settled four cents a barrel lower at $19.53. On London's IPE, May Brent ended five cents lower at $17.86 a barrel.
Dealers also noted the options expiry in May crude Friday had little impact on the contract, with most of the open interest in the $20.00 strike.
